extracted.intended_audience: science journalists and science communicators (especially those using embargoed material)
extracted.subtask_short: science journalism — embargoes and peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for science journalists on how embargoes, peer review, and preprints work, and how to ethically and rigorously use embargoed advance access and press releases when preparing coverage. Emphasises verification, context, and avoiding uncritical reliance on supplied materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review: purpose and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is a process in which two or three expert reviewers (not involved in the research) assess an article's rigour, novelty, scientific relevance and fit to the journal to decide whether it should be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat peer review as a guarantee of quality, irrefutability, or revealed truth. Use peer review status as an indicator that editors and reviewers found the work worthy of academic discussion, but continue to scrutinise methods, results, and claims when reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat preprints with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints (e.g., on medRxiv, bioRxiv, arXiv) are preliminary papers that have not passed peer review and can be uploaded with few or no controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report preprints carefully: clearly indicate their non–peer-reviewed status, avoid presenting conclusions as settled, and seek independent expert assessment before amplifying claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect embargoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists who contact and register with a journal can get prior access to papers under an embargo which they agree to respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat respecting embargoes as a professional responsibility — it permits advance preparation and access; breaking embargoes can result in loss of access to platforms and materials. Balance respect for embargoes with the need to verify and contextualise findings ethically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use embargo time to verify and enrich coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargoes are intended to give journalists enough advance time to prepare stories: to interview authors, cross-check with independent sources, and produce rigorous, attractive content without rushing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When given embargoed access, prioritise independent verification, interviews with authors and external experts, and deeper reporting rather than simply reproducing supplied materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uncritical reliance on press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases from research centres and journals are useful and informative but are always partial information and produced by communication staff with an interest in promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not simply translate or copy press releases. Treat them as starting points: check claims against the paper, seek independent commentary, and highlight limitations and context to avoid uncritical science journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of agenda-setting and selection bias
rubrics_metrics.description: There is criticism that by deciding which research merits press releases and embargoed promotion, journals and research centres can set the agenda for science coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek original stories and diverse sources beyond what is promoted by journals to counteract agenda-setting. Question whether studied topics are genuinely newsworthy beyond promotional emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise newsroom constraints as an anti-pattern risk
rubrics_metrics.description: In media organisations with few science editors or precarious working conditions, embargoed materials can enable reactive, passive coverage where outlets copy press releases instead of doing original reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In constrained environments, be especially vigilant about independent verification and avoid the easy path of reproducing press-release content; strive for added value even under resource limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand embargo platforms and supplied materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Major platforms (e.g., EurekAlert!, Springer Nature) provide embargoed papers along with press releases, researcher contacts, artwork and sometimes press conferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these materials as resources (paper PDFs, contacts, images) but remain critical of their framing; follow up with independent experts and verify any promotional claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label and contextualise the study's status and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies may be preprints or peer-reviewed articles; peer review does not equal infallibility and press materials are partial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always indicate whether the work is peer-reviewed or a preprint, explain the review status and known limitations, and convey uncertainty rather than overstating findings.
